note: Places for medieval and fantasy towns. An entry with `eras` is only for those eras; `water` only where the place has that water.

places.summary: A low-beamed alehouse with rushes on the floor, a fire that never quite goes out and the same six regulars on the same bench.
A noisy alehouse where carters and drovers drink, dice and argue over the price of wool.
An alewife's front room with a bush hung over the door to say the new brew is ready.
Just inside the town gate, the first drink for anyone coming in from the road and the last for anyone leaving.
A vaulted cellar under a merchant's house, lit by tallow candles, where apprentices go when their masters are abed.
Watermen and fishers drink here with their boots still wet and the tide table chalked on the wall.
A smoky harbour tavern full of sailors' songs and strangers' coin, with a back room nobody admits to.
Known for its minstrels, who play for their supper on a stool by the hearth most nights.
Adventurers, sellswords and hedge-wizards trade stories and job offers over cheap mead.
A dwarf-run alehouse with stone tables, dark beer brewed underground and a strict rule about singing.
Brewing in the yard and a skittle alley out back; the landlord's dog decides who is welcome.
Sells the abbey's own ale through a hatch in the wall, and nobody asks too many questions about it.
The best inn in town, with a galleried yard, stabling for forty horses and featherbeds for those who can pay.
A plain inn for pedlars and pilgrims: a shared bed, a bowl of pottage and a place by the fire.
A rambling timber inn on the market place where merchants strike deals over roast capon and spiced wine.
Kept by the abbey for travellers, with a hall of long tables and a lay brother who sings grace too slowly.
Ship's masters lodge here between voyages, and the window seats look straight out over the moorings.
A tall inn with an elven innkeeper who remembers every guest who ever stayed, and when.
A roadside inn where the carriers' carts stop, with a cook famous for her eel pie.
Over the bridge, the inn where wedding feasts and guild dinners are held in the long upstairs room.
Stalls round the market cross every Thursday: cheeses, eggs, cloth, pots, a tooth-drawer and a man selling relics of doubtful saints.
A narrow street of butchers' stalls with overhanging upper floors, loud with cleavers before dawn.
Fishwives cry the morning catch from stone slabs by the water, and gulls take whatever they leave.
Farmers bring sacks of grain to sell by the bushel under the open-sided market house.
The town's bakehouse, where people bring their own dough to bake and buy hot loaves and pies at the door.
An open field where the drovers' fair and the hiring fair are held, empty the rest of the year but for geese.
Lantern-lit stalls of charms, spiced cakes, potion vials and enchanted trinkets that rarely work twice.
Wise women and gardeners sell herbs, simples and cures, each swearing hers is the only one that works.
The cobbled heart of town, with the pillory, the well, the proclamation post and everyone's business.
A village green with a maypole, a pond and grazing rights that three families have argued over for a century.
Where bulls were once baited and now the mummers play, the ballad sellers sing and the town crier shouts the news.
The churchyard where people meet after mass, sit on the old tombs and settle disputes before the priest notices.
A paved court round a carved fountain said to grant one wish a lifetime, so nobody uses theirs.
A covered stone cross where butter, eggs and milk are sold, and where courting couples arrange to meet.
The parish church, with a squat tower, painted walls of saints and devils, and a bell rung for every death in the parish.
A great abbey church whose monks sing the hours day and night; the town grew up around its gates.
A tiny chapel on the bridge where travellers light a candle and pay a penny for a safe road.
Barefoot friars preach in the yard, feed the poor at the gate and quarrel with the parish priest.
A spring under a little stone hood, hung with rags and ribbons left by those hoping for a cure.
A circular temple open to the sky, where priestesses read omens in the night and bless newborns at dawn.
A ring of old standing stones in a grove, older than the town, where offerings still appear on midsummer morning.
A small priory of nuns who keep bees, teach girls their letters and brew a cordial they sell at the gate.
Where the merchant guild meets, fixes prices and holds a feast every year that the whole town hears about.
The weavers' guild hall, where cloth is measured, sealed and fined if it is short.
The smiths' and armourers' hall, hung with old weapons and the guild's banner of three hammers.
The timbered hall over the market where the reeve holds court, collects tolls and hears every complaint.
The guild of licensed spellcasters, who register familiars, settle hex disputes and fine unlicensed fortune-tellers.
The brewers' guild, where the ale-taster passes or fails every brew and the losers drink their own.
A smithy that rings from first light: horseshoes, nails, hinges and whatever the castle needs mended today.
Three looms clacking in a front room, with the family spinning in the back and children winding bobbins.
Tan pits by the water, so foul that the town made them move downwind, twice.
A potter's yard with a kiln smoking day and night and rows of jugs drying on planks in the sun.
A carpenter's shop that builds everything from cradles to coffins, smelling of sawdust and pitch.
Vats of woad, madder and weld; the dyers' hands are blue to the elbow and the stream runs a different colour each day.
Scribes copying books, letters and leases by the window light, with a boy grinding ink in the corner.
A water mill grinding the town's corn, the miller taking his toll and everybody sure he takes too much.
A chandler's shop making tallow candles for the poor and wax ones for the church, sold by the pound.
Boats on the stocks, the smell of tar and new oak, and shipwrights who whistle the same tune for a week.
Glass alembics bubbling in the window and the occasional small explosion; the neighbours have stopped complaining.
Bell-founders casting church bells in a pit, with half the town turning out to hear a new one rung.
A stone quay where boats unload salt fish, wine and wool, and porters run with bales on their backs.
A walled harbour full of cogs and fishing boats, with the harbour master counting every barrel that lands.
Wooden landing stages on the river where barges load timber and grain for the towns downstream.
A ferryman's landing with a bell to ring for him, and a bench where people wait and swap news.
A shingle beach where fishing boats are hauled up, nets hung to dry and the catch sold straight off the boat.
Where the king's men weigh wool for export and collect the duty, watched by sullen merchants.
Walled herb beds the monks tend, with a fishpond, beehives and a bench in the sun for the old brothers.
Old apple and pear trees inside the walls, where the household walks on summer evenings.
Terraced vines on the south slope, with a press-house and a harvest feast that ends in dancing.
A garden of silver flowers that only open at night, tended by an elf who never says who planted it.
A formal garden of knot beds and clipped box, opened to the townsfolk on feast days.
Long plots of cabbages, leeks and beans outside the walls, each family's patch marked with a stake.
The castle on the rise, its keep and curtain wall watching over every roof in town.
A many-arched stone bridge lined with little shops and houses, so narrow two carts cannot pass.
The walls and gatehouse, with a walk along the top where lovers meet and the watch pretends not to see.
A bare hill above town with the beacon ready to light, and a view to three counties on a clear day.
A crooked tower with no door anyone has found; lights move in its windows on moonless nights.
A broken keep from older wars, ivy to the battlements, where children dare each other to climb.
A fire tower on the headland kept burning by the monks, the last thing sailors see and the first.
Huge pale bones half buried on the hillside, which the old folk swear belonged to the last dragon in the land.
The tower over the market with the great bell that rings curfew, when every fire must be covered.
Common land where everyone may graze a cow, gather furze and fly a falcon, and where the fair comes in summer.
The field where every man must practise his archery on Sundays, and where the young ones show off.
Flat meadows by the river, flooded in winter and full of buttercups and picnics by June.
A walled deer park outside town where the lord hunts and the townsfolk may walk the rides on feast days.
A meadow ringed with toadstools where children are warned not to dance after dark, and always do.
The old track out of town along the ridge, worn deep by centuries of pilgrims and drovers.
The path beside the river where the barge horses walk and anglers sit, and courting couples go further than they meant to.
A road under old oaks into the forest, where woodcutters work and travellers hurry before dusk.
A path along the cliff tops with the sea far below and samphire gatherers dangling on ropes.
A path into the old wood that seems a little longer every time you walk it.
A path round the lake through reeds and alders, with herons, a hermit's hut and a lot of mud.
The lord's great hall, where feasts, dancing and mummers' plays are held and townsfolk may watch from the screens.
A galleried inn yard where travelling players put on their plays from a cart, and the audience joins in.
A sunken ring for cockfights and wrestling bouts, loud with wagers on market days.
Where the bards' college holds its contests; the winner's song is sung in every tavern for a year.
The jousting ground below the castle, with stands for the gentry and a rope for everyone else.
Books chained to oak desks in a long quiet room; you may read if a monk vouches for you.
Shelves of scrolls and spellbooks tended by a sleepy archivist and a sharper-eyed cat.
A handful of books the grammar school lends out, and a master who wants each one back by Sunday.
A cookshop selling hot roast meat, pasties and pottage from a counter, so people who have no oven can eat hot.
Eel pies, mutton pies and pies of uncertain filling, sold through the window with a ladle of gravy.
An ordinary where a fixed meal is served at one long table at noon, and you eat whatever is set down.
Seven meals a day, each better than the last, in a round-doored kitchen with low ceilings and enormous portions.
Fried and stewed fish from the morning's catch, eaten at trestle tables by the water.
Rich travellers dine here on dishes spiced with pepper, saffron and cinnamon brought from the far side of the world.
A quiet tea house with paper lanterns, little cakes and a game of stones in the corner that never seems to end.
A front room selling honey cakes, mead by the cup and posset to anyone with a cold.
A wafer-maker's stall where hot spiced wafers come off the irons all morning, eaten standing in the street.
Public baths with wooden tubs and steam rooms, a barber who bleeds and shaves, and a reputation it is trying to live down.
A fencing master's yard where squires and townsmen learn the longsword and limp home bruised.
A ring of trampled grass where young men wrestle for a ram on feast days and practise the rest of the year.
A railed-off stretch of shallows where people swim on hot days and the brave go in all year round.
Jars of dried herbs, powdered stones and syrups behind a counter, and a stuffed crocodile hanging from the beam.
Silks, velvets and fine linen for those who can afford them, measured out by the ell on a long counter.
Goldsmiths and moneychangers in a row of narrow shops, with a watchman at each end of the street.
Cheap stalls of ribbons, buckles, needles and ballad sheets, and a pedlar who will sell you anything twice.
Wands, enchanted thimbles, maps that redraw themselves and a shopkeeper who never quite gives a straight answer.
A stationer selling parchment, ink, primers, saints' lives and almanacs from a booth by the church door.
Shoes horses and doctors every animal in town, from plough oxen to the alewife's lapdog.
